The clinical presentation is dominated by a rapidly progressive (3-month gait decline to wheelchair dependence), multisystem neurodegenerative syndrome involving the cerebellum (gait ataxia, dysarthria), brainstem (dysarthria, possible oculomotor or bulbar involvement implied by “prominent cerebellar–brainstem–basal ganglia involvement”), and basal ganglia (implied by inclusion in exam findings and MRI abnormalities). Urinary incontinence — present for 1 year — is an early and prominent autonomic feature. Critically, there is *no subjective sensory loss, no limb weakness, no bowel dysfunction, no visual disturbance, no seizures, no movement disorder* (e.g., tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, myoclonus) — which argues against many mimics: not typical of hereditary ataxias (which usually spare bladder early), not consistent with inflammatory/demyelinating disease (no optic neuritis, no sensory symptoms, no CSF pleocytosis expected), and lacks red flags for paraneoplastic or infectious etiologies (no fever, cognitive change, seizures, or systemic symptoms).

Multiple System Atrophy, cerebellar subtype (MSA-C)

[THOUGHT]  
The clinical presentation is dominated by a rapidly progressive (3-month gait decline to wheelchair dependence), multisystem neurodegenerative syndrome involving the cerebellum (gait ataxia, dysarthria), brainstem (dysarthria, possible oculomotor or bulbar involvement implied by “prominent cerebellar–brainstem–basal ganglia involvement”), and basal ganglia (implied by inclusion in exam findings and MRI abnormalities). Urinary incontinence — present for 1 year — is an early and prominent autonomic feature. Critically, there is *no subjective sensory loss, no limb weakness, no bowel dysfunction, no visual disturbance, no seizures, no movement disorder* (e.g., tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, myoclonus) — which argues against many mimics: not typical of hereditary ataxias (which usually spare bladder early), not consistent with inflammatory/demyelinating disease (no optic neuritis, no sensory symptoms, no CSF pleocytosis expected), and lacks red flags for paraneoplastic or infectious etiologies (no fever, cognitive change, seizures, or systemic symptoms).  

MRI shows *multifocal atrophy and signal abnormalities specifically in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia* — highly characteristic of Multiple System Atrophy (MSA), particularly the cerebellar subtype (MSA-C), where hot cross bun sign (pontine atrophy + cruciform hyperintensity on T2/FLAIR), middle cerebellar peduncle (MCP) hyperintensity, and putaminal hypointensity with lateral rim hyperintensity are classic. The rapid progression (wheelchair in 3 months), early urinary incontinence (1 year prior), and dysarthria align strongly with MSA rather than slower-progressing SCAs (e.g., SCA6 typically has pure cerebellar syndrome over decades; SCA2/3 may have autonomic features but rarely this fulminant a course without prominent neuropathy or parkinsonism). PSP is unlikely without vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, early falls, or cognitive/behavioral changes — none reported. ILOCA is a diagnosis of exclusion and does not explain the *basal ganglia involvement* or *early severe autonomic failure*. The absence of documented parkinsonism does not exclude MSA-P or MSA-C — parkinsonism may be subtle or masked by ataxia; moreover, urinary incontinence often precedes motor features in MSA.  

Pending tests are appropriate but none contradict MSA: B12/copper/ceruloplasmin rule out treatable mimics; CSF will likely be normal (MSA is not inflammatory); anti-AQP4/MOG are negative in MSA; NfL is elevated in many neurodegenerative diseases including MSA; genetic testing is essential to exclude SCA2/3 but the *sporadic onset, rapid tempo, and autonomic prominence* make hereditary ataxia less likely — especially without family history (not mentioned). VLCFAs would screen for adrenoleukodystrophy, but that typically shows white matter FLAIR hyperintensity, not isolated brainstem/cerebellar/basal ganglia atrophy.

[EVIDENCE]  
- Progressive gait impairment leading to wheelchair dependence within 3 months  
- 1-year history of urinary incontinence (early and prominent autonomic dysfunction)  
- Recent onset of slurred speech (dysarthria), indicating brainstem/cerebellar-bulbar involvement  
- Neurological examination reveals prominent cerebellar–brainstem–basal ganglia involvement  
- Brain and spinal cord MRI shows multifocal atrophy and signal abnormalities in brainstem, cerebellum, and basal ganglia  
- No subjective sensory loss, limb weakness, bowel dysfunction, visual disturbance, seizures, or movement disorders — arguing against mimics like MS, vasculitis, paraneoplastic syndromes, or hereditary neuropathies  

[GAPS]  
- Detailed MRI report specifying presence/absence of classic MSA signs: hot cross bun sign, putaminal hypointensity with lateral rim hyperintensity, middle cerebellar peduncle hyperintensity, or “slit-like” putaminal atrophy  
- Formal autonomic testing results (e.g., orthostatic BP drop, urodynamic studies) to confirm severity and distribution of autonomic failure  
- Family history — not explicitly stated; critical to assess likelihood of hereditary ataxia  
- Age of onset — not provided; MSA is typically >50 years; younger onset would increase suspicion for SCA2/3/FXN  
- Presence/absence of objective parkinsonism (e.g., rigidity, bradykinesia, rest tremor) on exam — not specified, only “no movement disorders” subjectively reported  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Multiple System Atrophy, cerebellar subtype (MSA-C)
